to be or not to be like Jensen Huang?

1963
- he was born in Tainan

1973
- his parents sent him to the US at 9 with his older brother to live with their uncle.
- his uncle thought he had found them a good boarding school, but it was a reform school in Kentucky.
- his daily job there was cleaning the toilets.
- his roommate was 17 and had knife scars from fights.
- Jensen taught him to read, and in return he taught Jensen to bench press.
- he also picked up table tennis there and got good enough to be nationally ranked as a teenager.

late 1970s
- his family reunited in Oregon.
- he worked at Denny's as a dishwasher and busboy while he was in high school.
- he skipped two grades and finished high school at 16.

1984
- he graduated in electrical engineering from Oregon State.
- his lab partner there was Lori, and he later married her.
- he went on to design chips at AMD and then at LSI Logic.

1992
- he finished a master's at Stanford while working full time.
- he started meeting two engineers, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, at a Denny's in San Jose to plan a company.

1993
- he turned 30 and they started NVIDIA.

1995
- their first chip, the NV1, flopped.

1996
- the chip they were building for Sega's next console didn't work either.
- he told Sega they couldn't deliver, and asked them to invest anyway.
- Sega put in $5M, which he later said was all the money they had.
- he laid off more than half the company, going from about 100 people to 40.
- for years after that, he opened meetings with "our company is 30 days from going out of business".

1997
- their next chip, the RIVA 128, sold 1 million units in its first 4 months.

1999
- NVIDIA went public at $12 a share.
- they launched the GeForce 256 and called it the world's first GPU.

2000
- Microsoft picked NVIDIA to make the graphics chip for the first Xbox.

2006
- they launched CUDA so their chips could do more than games.

2008
- the market didn't understand CUDA, and NVIDIA fell below $5 billion during the financial crisis.

2012
- AlexNet, the model that kicked off modern AI, was trained on 2 NVIDIA gaming cards.

2016
- he hand-delivered his first AI supercomputer to a small nonprofit called OpenAI.

2019
- he bought the networking company Mellanox for $6.9B.

2020
- he agreed to buy Arm for $40B, and regulators killed the deal in 2022.

2022
- the stock dropped about 50% that year.
- ChatGPT launched in November, trained on NVIDIA chips.

2023
- NVIDIA hit $1 trillion.
- when someone asked if he'd start NVIDIA again, he said "I wouldn't do it".

2024
- NVIDIA passed $3 trillion and briefly became the most valuable company in the world.

2025
- in July it became the first company ever to hit $4 trillion.
- in October it became the first to hit $5 trillion.

October 2026
- the NYT reported that he was close to a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese spy.
- NVIDIA said his dealings with her were "not unusual or unexpected".

November 2026
- 3 House committee chairs asked him to explain his ties to her in a closed-door briefing.
- 3 days later he admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife.
- the board opened an investigation.
- the NYT then reported a second alleged affair, with an NVIDIA executive who reports to him.
- the WSJ reported that the board was getting ready to push him out.
- the stock kept falling.
- on November 12 he resigned as CEO, 33 years after he started NVIDIA.
- within hours, NVIDIA lost as much as $600 billion in value, before closing the day down 4.3%.
- the same day, Reuters reported a third alleged affair, with another NVIDIA employee.

so, to be or not to be like Jensen Huang?

hits.draft_en:
Jensen Huang's life reads like two different movies.

Movie one: born in Tainan in 1963, sent to the US at 9, and accidentally enrolled in a Kentucky reform school where his chore was scrubbing toilets. Later a Denny's busboy in Oregon, out of high school at 16, then electrical engineering at Oregon State and chip design at AMD and LSI Logic.

NVIDIA was planned over Denny's tables in San Jose and founded in 1993. The NV1 flopped, the Sega chip failed, Sega put in $5M anyway, and headcount fell from about 100 to 40. Then came the RIVA 128, the 1999 IPO at $12, the GeForce 256 billed as the first GPU, CUDA, AlexNet trained on 2 gaming cards, and an AI supercomputer hand-delivered to OpenAI. $1 trillion in 2023, then $4 trillion and $5 trillion in 2025.

Movie two: the spy report in October 2026, the admitted affair in November 2026, a board investigation, two more alleged affairs, and on November 12 his resignation as CEO after 33 years.

So - would you want to be Jensen Huang?

It feels like a BTC confidence crash not a price one.

For vibe-memecoins like BTC, price is the product and the lower the price goes the weaker the belief in it's SoV story.

The current dump is especially painful as many believed $58k was the bottom and failure to retrace while AI stocks bounce backed hurt badly.

So BTC continues to dump without significant dip buyers who end up buying AI crash than crypto.

Obviously, if BTC drops significantly lower the dip buyers will appear chasing a bounce back.

But those might be short-term traders instead of buying for long-term hold.

Previously, on dips like this CT would be full with bull-posters sharing their sound-money thesis with perhaps too delusional takes. They lifted the spirits.

Now it's All Quiet on the Western Front

Based from ppl I talk to and on sentiment on X, BTC simply isn't as exciting as it used to be.

Previously BTC maxis are selling some BTC for ZEC or even PRL as a hedge if BTC fails.

BTC FAILURE WAS NOT AN OPTION FOR OG MAXIS! That is the confidence shake up I feel.

And with ETFs BTC is becoming like a 'boomer' coin but without boomers actually significantly allocating to it (judging from ETF flows).

Worrying are stablecoin outflows, MSTR excluded from MSCI. The lower the BTC goes, the stronger the MSTR FUD will get.

I'd say the confidence crisis is more applicable to BTC as alts are holding surprisingly well vs BTC. The pet-rock just drags everything down.

Crypto still has a long road of adoption ahead of us: don't forget about recent HYPE and AVAX partnerships.

But these partnerships have little to do with BTC as BTC isn't a great trade for overall crypto adoption anymore.

So I wish other alts stopped trading with BTC on the way down as well.

Hope I'm wrong and my bearish bias is talking here and X algo just fails to show bullish posts to me.

Looking for your -non AI- counter arguments in the comments.

hits.name: Zach Lloyd
hits.text:
Speaking at @aiDotEngineer Code Summit SF, the "software factory stack" seemed to resonate. Here's a breakdown of the components:

00 – Factories-as-code. Every aspect of the factory (agent workflows, access permissions, cloud sandbox configuration, and so on) should be version-controlled code that humans and agents can modify.

01 – Data & Context. You should own all of the data your agent interacts with on your own infrastructure. Your internal skills and MCPs, agent traces, access logs, telemetry... everything.

02 – Compute. Agents should have their own computer, with controlled sandbox permissions and support for multiple operating systems. This should be self-hostable.

03 – Inference. You should have access to any model and any harness to benchmark the right match for your setup. Don't lock in to any one model provider.

04 – Improvement. You (and agents) need tools to measure and improve your factory. This means observability over cost-per-PR, cycle times, latency, and other DORA metrics. It also means self-improvement, with agents scoring output quality, proposing changes to the factory, and re-measuring in a loop.

05 – Orchestration. You need a runtime to launch agents, track work, and recover from failures. It should also handle message passing between agents in a multi-agent system.

06 – Access. You should be able to connect the factory to any external system. You'll want an MCP server and REST API to access the factory itself, and integrations with where your team works (Slack, MS Teams, Jira, Linear, etc). We don't recommend an "ADE" or web interface that's tightly coupled to the factory.

Yet most business owners will NEVER set it up themselves.

I think there's a lot of money to be made here for AI consultants (just like there was in setting up Google Business profiles in the 2010s).

1. I'd lead with a free audit. Literally just ask ChatGPT about their business, open the profile, screenshot what's wrong or missing, then send it to them.

-Write the agent's instructions

-Fix every wrong answer

hits.text:
how to become a latency sniper on Polymarket. people make ~$500 a day on this in BTC 5m markets.

here's a step-by-step guide

it turned out simpler than i thought: grab the old price after a BTC jump and buy the other side when the market flips
  
his game plan:

1. every 5 minutes a new market opens: will BTC be higher or lower in 5 minutes 
  
2. the market moves on the BTC price from Chainlink. Chainlink collects the price from exchanges, averages it and feeds it to Polymarket
  
3. the early move shows up on Binance, and that's the signal to get in. BTC moves hard one way within 15-30 seconds, Polymarket still has the old price, and he buys that side right away
  
4. if BTC turns back, the other side gets cheaper. he buys it too, so the UP + DOWN pair costs him less than $1
  
5. he holds everything until the market ends or merges the pair back into $1. he never sells

where does the money come from?

about 70% comes from entries after a price jump. other buyers at the same price and the same time left lose ~3% on average after fees, he makes +10%

the other ~30% comes from pairs. UP + DOWN cost him 91¢ on average, and at resolve he gets $1

why does this even work?

say there are 3 minutes left. BTC is flat and UP trades at 50¢. then BTC jumps up on Binance. on Polymarket sellers keep their orders at 50-55¢ for a bit longer, and he takes them.

in 6 out of 10 markets he holds UP until the end.

if BTC pulls back, DOWN drops to like 35¢ and he buys it. now he's got a pair for ~88¢, and at resolve he gets $1 whatever happens.

his trades are small, ~$6 on average, because he's not the only one sniping

here's his profile: https://t.co/tJta4UZglh

The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate.

Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine.

Enjoy!

virals.text:
Making the most AI pilled company is the whole game:

1. make a second brain. one folder of markdown files on how you think, write and decide (obsidian)

2. talk to it. voice notes all day (wispr), and an agent files every fact, story and decision

3. make a company brain. customers, calls, numbers, pricing, playbooks, past decisions and why you made them

4. record every call and meeting (granola). the transcripts go straight into the brain

5. keep a facts file. true things about you and the company that agents are allowed to say. this kills made-up claims

6. keep a voice file. your 50 best posts, 20 you hate, and the words you never use

7. put all of it in git (github) so every change has a history

8. write one instruction file at the top (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md). read these files before any task, never overwrite, always date

9. give agents memory across sessions so they stop starting from zero (claude-mem, mem0)

10. pipe every data source into one warehouse your agents can query (airbyte → clickhouse). ads, analytics, CRM, payments

11. feed it data nobody else has. it's the only part a competitor can't download

the skills

12. don't start from zero. install the good ones first (anthropics/skills, obra/superpowers, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills)

13. grab the marketing ones too (coreyhaines31/marketingskills, cody schneider's graphed skills for static ads and UGC, boringmarketing dot com skills)

14. map every workflow in the company and rank them by money made or saved

15. do each one once while talking out loud, and record it

16. have an agent turn the recording into a skill. when to use it, the steps, the checks, the mistakes to avoid

17. one skill per job. small and boring beats one giant prompt

18. connect your tools with MCPs so agents can act and not only advise (gmail, slack, stripe, linear, notion, posthog, supabase)

19. give agents a browser (browser-use, vercel agent-browser, claude in chrome)

20. give agents a computer of their own for the tools with no API (vercel agent-desktop, orgo)

21. give your best skills away in public. it's the new lead magnet

the agents

22. run an orchestrator that never turns off (grok bot, openclaw, hermes). it manages one agent per project, and each of those runs its own sub-agents

23. use coding agents for the building (claude code, codex, cursor, t3, antigravity)

24. wrap them in a harness so they plan, test and remember (ECC, superpowers)

25. manage the whole fleet in one place (paperclip). every agent gets a job, a budget and a log

26. put the skills on triggers (n8n, scheduled tasks). daily, weekly, on every new lead, on every cancellation

27. route your models (openrouter). the expensive one plans and checks (fable 5.2, gemini 4 carbon), the cheap ones do the volume

28. cut the token bill. shorter outputs, smaller tool results (caveman)

29. run a local model for the data that can't leave your machine (gemma 4)

30. track cost per job. if a job costs more than it earns, fix it or kill it

the factory

31. build the line. spec agent → builder agents in parallel (git worktrees) → test agent → reviewer agent → deploy (vercel, railway)

32. design goes through the same line (paper MCP), and a skill strips out anything that looks AI made (unslop)

33. every annoying task in the company becomes an internal tool by the end of the day

34. every customer request becomes a pull request before a human reads it (tstack for the PR workflow)

35. reviewer agents with a named bar. "would the best team in the world ship this?" reject until the answer is yes

36. keep 50 real cases with the right answer. rerun them every time a new model drops and switch to the winner

37. humans approve, own the outcome and talk to customers. that's the 10% you keep

the loop

38. every finished job writes back to the brain. what worked, what failed, what to stop doing

39. support tickets, analytics and social comments flow in every night

40. every friday an agent rewrites the playbooks from the week's results, and you approve the diff

41. every month, rank everything by profit per human hour. kill one thing and double one thing

the growth

42. research with agents before you spend a dollar (perplexity API, last30days skill)

43. outbound runs itself. find the leads, enrich, verify, send (apollo, million verifier, instantly, phantombuster)

44. send prospects finished work in place of a pitch

45. ads run on a loop. an agent writes the creative, publishes through the facebook ads API, kills the losers and scales the winners

46. agents make the creative too. images (nano banana), video (heygen, fal), voice (elevenlabs), music (lyria 3.5, suno)

47. turn every finished job into content. the story, the number, the prompt

48. every customer makes the brain smarter for the next one. that's your network effect

49. once it works, point it at a new niche. same agents, new context

The models are the same for everyone but your context is the only part that's yours.

Acquire as much of it as you can, as fast as you can.

Build loops like this.

This is the whole game, happy playing.

What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? 

The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate.

Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine.

Enjoy!

outsiders.name: GREG ISENBERG
outsiders.text:
Making the most AI pilled company is the whole game:

1. make a second brain. one folder of markdown files on how you think, write and decide (obsidian)

2. talk to it. voice notes all day (wispr), and an agent files every fact, story and decision

3. make a company brain. customers, calls, numbers, pricing, playbooks, past decisions and why you made them

4. record every call and meeting (granola). the transcripts go straight into the brain

5. keep a facts file. true things about you and the company that agents are allowed to say. this kills made-up claims

6. keep a voice file. your 50 best posts, 20 you hate, and the words you never use

7. put all of it in git (github) so every change has a history

8. write one instruction file at the top (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md). read these files before any task, never overwrite, always date

9. give agents memory across sessions so they stop starting from zero (claude-mem, mem0)

10. pipe every data source into one warehouse your agents can query (airbyte → clickhouse). ads, analytics, CRM, payments

11. feed it data nobody else has. it's the only part a competitor can't download

the skills

12. don't start from zero. install the good ones first (anthropics/skills, obra/superpowers, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills)

13. grab the marketing ones too (coreyhaines31/marketingskills, cody schneider's graphed skills for static ads and UGC, boringmarketing dot com skills)

14. map every workflow in the company and rank them by money made or saved

15. do each one once while talking out loud, and record it

16. have an agent turn the recording into a skill. when to use it, the steps, the checks, the mistakes to avoid

17. one skill per job. small and boring beats one giant prompt

18. connect your tools with MCPs so agents can act and not only advise (gmail, slack, stripe, linear, notion, posthog, supabase)

19. give agents a browser (browser-use, vercel agent-browser, claude in chrome)

20. give agents a computer of their own for the tools with no API (vercel agent-desktop, orgo)

21. give your best skills away in public. it's the new lead magnet

the agents

22. run an orchestrator that never turns off (grok bot, openclaw, hermes). it manages one agent per project, and each of those runs its own sub-agents

23. use coding agents for the building (claude code, codex, cursor, t3, antigravity)

24. wrap them in a harness so they plan, test and remember (ECC, superpowers)

25. manage the whole fleet in one place (paperclip). every agent gets a job, a budget and a log

26. put the skills on triggers (n8n, scheduled tasks). daily, weekly, on every new lead, on every cancellation

27. route your models (openrouter). the expensive one plans and checks (fable 5.2, gemini 4 carbon), the cheap ones do the volume

28. cut the token bill. shorter outputs, smaller tool results (caveman)

29. run a local model for the data that can't leave your machine (gemma 4)

30. track cost per job. if a job costs more than it earns, fix it or kill it

the factory

31. build the line. spec agent → builder agents in parallel (git worktrees) → test agent → reviewer agent → deploy (vercel, railway)

32. design goes through the same line (paper MCP), and a skill strips out anything that looks AI made (unslop)

33. every annoying task in the company becomes an internal tool by the end of the day

34. every customer request becomes a pull request before a human reads it (tstack for the PR workflow)

35. reviewer agents with a named bar. "would the best team in the world ship this?" reject until the answer is yes

36. keep 50 real cases with the right answer. rerun them every time a new model drops and switch to the winner

37. humans approve, own the outcome and talk to customers. that's the 10% you keep

the loop

38. every finished job writes back to the brain. what worked, what failed, what to stop doing

39. support tickets, analytics and social comments flow in every night

40. every friday an agent rewrites the playbooks from the week's results, and you approve the diff

41. every month, rank everything by profit per human hour. kill one thing and double one thing

the growth

42. research with agents before you spend a dollar (perplexity API, last30days skill)

43. outbound runs itself. find the leads, enrich, verify, send (apollo, million verifier, instantly, phantombuster)

44. send prospects finished work in place of a pitch

45. ads run on a loop. an agent writes the creative, publishes through the facebook ads API, kills the losers and scales the winners

46. agents make the creative too. images (nano banana), video (heygen, fal), voice (elevenlabs), music (lyria 3.5, suno)

47. turn every finished job into content. the story, the number, the prompt

48. every customer makes the brain smarter for the next one. that's your network effect

49. once it works, point it at a new niche. same agents, new context

The models are the same for everyone but your context is the only part that's yours.

Acquire as much of it as you can, as fast as you can.

Build loops like this.

This is the whole game, happy playing.

19. give agents a browser (browser-use, vercel agent-browser, claude in chrome)

20. give agents a computer of their own for the tools with no API (vercel agent-desktop, orgo)

21. give your best skills away in public. it's the new lead magnet

the agents

22. run an orchestrator that never turns off (grok bot, openclaw, hermes). it manages one agent per project, and each of those runs its own sub-agents

23. use coding agents for the building (claude code, codex, cursor, t3, antigravity)

24. wrap them in a harness so they plan, test and remember (ECC, superpowers)

25. manage the whole fleet in one place (paperclip). every agent gets a job, a budget and a log

26. put the skills on triggers (n8n, scheduled tasks). daily, weekly, on every new lead, on every cancellation

27. route your models (openrouter). the expensive one plans and checks (fable 5.2, gemini 4 carbon), the cheap ones do the volume

28. cut the token bill. shorter outputs, smaller tool results (caveman)

29. run a local model for the data that can't leave your machine (gemma 4)

30. track cost per job. if a job costs more than it earns, fix it or kill it

the factory

31. build the line. spec agent → builder agents in parallel (git worktrees) → test agent → reviewer agent → deploy (vercel, railway)

32. design goes through the same line (paper MCP), and a skill strips out anything that looks AI made (unslop)

33. every annoying task in the company becomes an internal tool by the end of the day

34. every customer request becomes a pull request before a human reads it (tstack for the PR workflow)

35. reviewer agents with a named bar. "would the best team in the world ship this?" reject until the answer is yes

36. keep 50 real cases with the right answer. rerun them every time a new model drops and switch to the winner

37. humans approve, own the outcome and talk to customers. that's the 10% you keep

the loop

38. every finished job writes back to the brain. what worked, what failed, what to stop doing

39. support tickets, analytics and social comments flow in every night

40. every friday an agent rewrites the playbooks from the week's results, and you approve the diff

41. every month, rank everything by profit per human hour. kill one thing and double one thing

the growth

42. research with agents before you spend a dollar (perplexity API, last30days skill)

43. outbound runs itself. find the leads, enrich, verify, send (apollo, million verifier, instantly, phantombuster)

44. send prospects finished work in place of a pitch

45. ads run on a loop. an agent writes the creative, publishes through the facebook ads API, kills the losers and scales the winners

46. agents make the creative too. images (nano banana), video (heygen, fal), voice (elevenlabs), music (lyria 3.5, suno)

47. turn every finished job into content. the story, the number, the prompt

48. every customer makes the brain smarter for the next one. that's your network effect

49. once it works, point it at a new niche. same agents, new context

The models are the same for everyone but your context is the only part that's yours.

Acquire as much of it as you can, as fast as you can.

Build loops like this.

This is the whole game, happy playing.
